claim: Complement dysregulation's direct contribution to the pathogenesis of peripheral nervous system diseases, including sensory neuropathies, is unclear.
source: Whether complement dysregulation directly contributes to the pathogenesis of peripheral nervous system diseases, including sensory neuropathies, is unclear.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of knowledge in the field as presented in the abstract, indicating a gap in understanding.

claim: C3 plays a central role in sensory nerve damage at the morphological and functional levels in a mouse model of ocular HSV-1 infection.
source: Through genetic and pharmacologic targeting, we uncovered a central role for C3 in sensory nerve damage at the morphological and functional levels.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from genetic (C3-/- mice) and pharmacologic (CVF treatment) approaches described in the manuscript.

claim: CD4 T cells are central in facilitating complement-mediated sensory nerve damage in ocular HSV-1 infection.
source: Interestingly, CD4 T cells were central in facilitating this complement-mediated damage.
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments and observations in TCRα-/- mice showing CD4 T cell requirement for sensation loss.

claim: The C3/CD4 T cell axis triggers corneal sensory nerve damage in a mouse model of ocular graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).
source: This same C3/CD4 T cell axis triggered corneal sensory nerve damage in a mouse model of ocular graft-versus-host disease (GVHD).
evidence: The manuscript presents experimental data from GVHD models showing C3 and CD4 T cell-dependent corneal sensation loss.

claim: The C3/CD4 T cell axis does not trigger corneal sensory nerve damage in a T-dependent allergic eye disease (AED) model.
source: However, this was not the case in a T-dependent allergic eye disease (AED) model, suggesting that this inflammatory neuroimmune pathology is specific to certain disease etiologies.
evidence: The AED model showed T cell infiltration but no corneal sensation loss, demonstrating context-specificity.

claim: This inflammatory neuroimmune pathology is specific to certain disease etiologies.
source: However, this was not the case in a T-dependent allergic eye disease (AED) model, suggesting that this inflammatory neuroimmune pathology is specific to certain disease etiologies.
evidence: The differential outcomes in AED versus HSV-1 and GVHD models support context-dependent mechanisms.

claim: Complement-targeted therapeutics may mitigate sensory neuropathies.
source: Collectively, these findings uncover a central role for complement in CD4 T cell-dependent corneal nerve damage in multiple disease settings and indicate the possibility for complement-targeted therapeutics to mitigate sensory neuropathies.
evidence: CVF treatment preserved corneal sensation in HSV-1 and GVHD models, providing proof of concept.

claim: Dysregulated complement activation is increasingly recognized as a significant pathological event in a variety of neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory diseases of the central nervous system.
source: Dysregulated complement activation is increasingly recognized as a significant pathological event in a variety of neurodegenerative and neuroinflammatory diseases of the central nervous system (Tenner et al., 2018).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tenner et al., 2018.

claim: Complement may orchestrate peripheral nervous system (PNS) disorders including nociceptive hypersensitivities, sensory neuropathies, and Guillain-Barré syndrome.
source: Complement may orchestrate peripheral nervous system (PNS) disorders as well. For instance, nociceptive hypersensitivities, sensory neuropathies, and Guillain-Barré syndrome have been linked to aberrant complement activation (Rosoklija et al., 2000; Ramaglia et al., 2008; Jang et al., 2010; Fritzinger and Benjamin, 2016; Xu et al., 2018; Susuki et al., 2007).
evidence: Multiple citations support the link between complement and various PNS disorders.

claim: The mechanistic role of complement is not well understood in neuroinflammatory pathologies impacting the PNS.
source: However, the mechanistic role of complement is not well understood in neuroinflammatory pathologies impacting the PNS.
evidence: This reflects the current state of knowledge and identifies a research gap.

claim: The pathophysiological trigger of sensory fiber retraction which contributes to sensation loss and in some instances chronic pain is unclear.
source: Moreover, the pathophysiological trigger of sensory fiber retraction which contributes to sensation loss and in some instances chronic pain is unclear (Stepp et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Available treatments for peripheral neuropathies primarily focus on clinical symptoms without addressing the underlying pathomechanisms.
source: Available treatments for peripheral neuropathies primarily focus on clinical symptoms without addressing the underlying pathomechanisms (Colloca et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Colloca et al., 2017.

claim: The complement cascade pivots upon activation of complement component 3 (C3) for its downstream proinflammatory effects.
source: The complement cascade pivots upon activation of complement component 3 (C3) for its downstream proinflammatory effects.
evidence: This reflects established scientific knowledge about the complement cascade.

claim: The eye has been labeled a 'complement dysregulation hotspot' due to complement's contributions to many ophthalmic diseases.
source: The eye has been labeled a 'complement dysregulation hotspot' due to complement's contributions to many ophthalmic diseases, but complement activation is restricted in the healthy cornea (Clark and Bishop, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clark and Bishop, 2018.

claim: Complement activation is restricted in the healthy cornea.
source: The eye has been labeled a 'complement dysregulation hotspot' due to complement's contributions to many ophthalmic diseases, but complement activation is restricted in the healthy cornea (Clark and Bishop, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Clark and Bishop, 2018.

claim: Corneal nerves are increasingly recognized as central regulators of immune privilege at the ocular surface.
source: Furthermore, corneal nerves are increasingly recognized as central regulators of immune privilege at the ocular surface (Guzmán et al., 2018; Neelam et al., 2018; Paunicka et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Inflammatory events that damage corneal nerves can have insidious consequences in terms of ocular surface health and transparency.
source: Consequently, inflammatory events that damage corneal nerves can have insidious consequences in terms of ocular surface health and transparency (Müller et al., 2003; Shaheen et al., 2014; Stepp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Corneal nerves originate predominantly from the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal ganglion (TG).
source: Corneal nerves originate predominantly from the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal ganglion (TG), and these peripheral nerves provide the cornea with the highest density of sensory fibers in the human body.
evidence: This reflects established anatomical knowledge.

claim: Peripheral nerves provide the cornea with the highest density of sensory fibers in the human body.
source: Corneal nerves originate predominantly from the ophthalmic branch of the trigeminal ganglion (TG), and these peripheral nerves provide the cornea with the highest density of sensory fibers in the human body.
evidence: This reflects established anatomical knowledge.

claim: The cornea and peripheral nerves constitutively synthesize complement proteins.
source: While the cornea and peripheral nerves constitutively synthesize complement proteins (Bora et al., 2008; de Jonge et al., 2004), the role of the complement cascade in corneal nerve damage has not been explored.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bora et al., 2008 and de Jonge et al., 2004.

claim: The role of the complement cascade in corneal nerve damage has not been explored.
source: While the cornea and peripheral nerves constitutively synthesize complement proteins (Bora et al., 2008; de Jonge et al., 2004), the role of the complement cascade in corneal nerve damage has not been explored.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The complement pathway is poised for vigorous activation in the cornea in response to noxious or inflammatory stimuli.
source: Nonetheless, the complement pathway is poised for vigorous activation in the cornea in response to noxious or inflammatory stimuli (Bora et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bora et al., 2008.

claim: C3 activation has been reported in the cornea soon after infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1).
source: Moreover, C3 activation has been reported in the cornea soon after infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), which is a common cause of corneal sensory nerve damage in patients (Royer et al., 2017; Sacchetti and Lambiase, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Royer et al., 2017 and Sacchetti and Lambiase, 2014.

claim: HSV-1 is a common cause of corneal sensory nerve damage in patients.
source: Moreover, C3 activation has been reported in the cornea soon after infection with herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1), which is a common cause of corneal sensory nerve damage in patients (Royer et al., 2017; Sacchetti and Lambiase, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Royer et al., 2017 and Sacchetti and Lambiase, 2014.

claim: Progressive loss of corneal mechano-sensitivity was evident in WT mice by days 5 to 8 post-infection with HSV-1.
source: Progressive loss of corneal mechano-sensitivity was evident in WT mice by days 5 to 8 p.i., but corneal sensation was conserved in the C3-/- cohort (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Corneal sensation was conserved in C3-/- mice following HSV-1 infection.
source: Progressive loss of corneal mechano-sensitivity was evident in WT mice by days 5 to 8 p.i., but corneal sensation was conserved in the C3-/- cohort (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: On day 3 post-infection, the HSV-1 burden was similar in the tear film, corneas, and TG of WT and C3-/- animals.
source: On day 3 p.i., the HSV-1 burden was similar in the tear film, corneas, and TG of WT and C3-/- animals (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: This is supported by viral titer measurements shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claim: By day 7 post-infection, HSV-1 titers were elevated in the tear film and TG of C3-/- mice relative to WT.
source: By day 7 p.i., HSV-1 titers were elevated in the tear film and TG of C3-/- mice relative to WT (Figure 1C,E).
evidence: This is supported by viral titer measurements shown in Figures 1C and 1E.

claim: Corneal buttons from WT mice exhibited extensive denervation with CD3+ T cell infiltration at day 8 post-infection.
source: Corneal buttons from WT mice exhibited extensive denervation with CD3+ T cell infiltration at day 8 p.i. (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1F.

claim: T cell infiltration was observed without widespread denervation in C3-/- corneas at day 8 post-infection.
source: However, T cell infiltration was observed without widespread denervation in C3-/- corneas (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The number of cornea-infiltrating CD4+ or CD8+ T cells were similar among WT and C3-/- mice.
source: The number of cornea-infiltrating CD4+ or CD8+ T cells were similar among WT and C3-/- mice (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Corneal sensation loss in herpetic keratitis involves a C3-dependent inflammatory process independent of viral burden.
source: Together, these data indicate that corneal sensation loss in herpetic keratitis involves a C3-dependent inflammatory process independent of viral burden.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the observation that C3-/- mice maintain sensation despite similar or higher viral loads.

claim: Chemokines associated with T cell recruitment were elevated in corneas from both WT and C3-/- mice at day 5 post-infection.
source: Chemokines associated with T cell recruitment were elevated in corneas from both WT and C3-/- mice at day 5 p.i.—a time consistent with onset of sensation loss (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by chemokine measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: CD4+ and CD8+ T cell expansion was comparable within the eye-draining mandibular lymph nodes (MLN) from WT and C3-/- mice.
source: Moreover, CD4+ and CD8+ T cell expansion was comparable within the eye-draining mandibular lymph nodes (MLN) from WT and C3-/- mice (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: T cells harvested from WT and C3-/- mice at day 8 post-infection responded equally to in vitro stimulation in terms of IFNγ production.
source: Similarly, T cells harvested from WT and C3-/- mice at day 8 p.i. responded equally to in vitro stimulation in terms of IFNγ production (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by in vitro stimulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: C3-/- T cells exhibit normal expansion and recruitment to the cornea during ocular HSV-1 infection.
source: Collectively, these data show that C3-/- T cells exhibit normal expansion and recruitment to the cornea during ocular HSV-1 infection.
evidence: This conclusion is based on chemokine, T cell expansion, and functional data from Figures 2A-C.

claim: Frank corneal sensation loss was not observed following ocular HSV-1 infection in C3-sufficient, alpha-beta T cell receptor-deficient mice (TCRα-/-).
source: In support of our hypothesis that C3 and T cells jointly coordinate corneal sensation loss, frank corneal sensation loss was not observed following ocular HSV-1 infection in C3-sufficient, alpha-beta T cell receptor-deficient mice (TCRα-/-) which congenitally lack classical CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by corneal sensation measurements in TCRα-/- mice shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Adoptive transfer of CD3+ T cells from either WT or C3-/- donors evoked progressive corneal sensation loss in TCRα-/- recipients by day 8 post-infection.
source: Adoptive transfer of CD3+ T cells from either WT or C3-/- donors evoked progressive corneal sensation loss in TCRα-/- recipients by day 8 p.i. (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 2D.

claim: C3-/- T cells remain functional in vivo.
source: These findings further corroborate that C3-/- T cells remain functional in vivo.
evidence: This conclusion is based on the adoptive transfer experiments showing C3-/- T cells can induce sensation loss.

claim: C3 and T cells are individually necessary and interdependent in the pathogenesis of HSV-1-associated corneal sensation loss.
source: Our collective findings reveal that C3 and T cells are individually necessary and interdependent in the pathogenesis of HSV-1-associated corneal sensation loss.
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings from C3-/- mice, TCRα-/- mice, and adoptive transfer experiments.

claim: C3 activation and T cell engagement coordinate corneal nerve damage in herpetic keratitis.
source: Whether by direct or indirect mechanisms, these data support a paradigm in which C3 activation and T cell engagement coordinate corneal nerve damage in herpetic keratitis.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the experimental findings presented in the manuscript.

claim: Corneal sensation loss during acute HSV-1 infection was only observed upon reconstitution with CD4+ T cells in TCRα-/- mice.
source: Corneal sensation loss during acute HSV-1 infection was only observed upon reconstitution with CD4+ T cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Transgenic OT-II mice did not exhibit corneal sensation loss following HSV-1 infection despite evidence of bystander CD4+ T cell activation and recruitment into the cornea.
source: Transgenic OT-II mice did not exhibit corneal sensation loss following infection despite evidence of bystander CD4+ T cell activation and recruitment into the cornea (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: This is supported by data from OT-II mice shown in Figures 3B-D.

claim: Active corneal HSV-1 infection was necessary to provoke corneal sensation loss in TCRα-/- mice reconstituted with CD4+ T cells.
source: Nonetheless, active corneal HSV-1 infection was necessary to provoke corneal sensation loss, as TCRα-/- mice reconstituted with CD4+ T cells harvested from HSV-infected WT mice did not elicit auto/allo-antigen-associated sensation loss within two weeks of corneal scratch injury (i.e. mock infection) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is supported by mock infection experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Complement C3 and antigen-specific CD4+ T cells are simultaneously necessary to drive corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection.
source: Collectively, our data show that complement C3 and antigen-specific CD4+ T cells are simultaneously necessary to drive corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection.
evidence: This conclusion integrates findings from C3-/-, TCRα-/-, and OT-II experiments.

claim: A coordinated inflammatory axis exists involving C3 and antigen-specific CD4+ T cells that is responsible for sensory neuropathy in herpetic keratitis.
source: These results strongly portend that a coordinated inflammatory axis exists involving C3 and antigen-specific CD4+ T cells, and that it is responsible for sensory neuropathy in herpetic keratitis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective experimental findings.

claim: Upregulation of complement effectors and anaphylatoxin receptors including C3, C5, C3ar1, and C5ar1 was noted in HSV-infected corneas.
source: Upregulation of complement effectors and anaphylatoxin receptors were noted including C3, C5, C3ar1, and C5ar1 (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Figures 4A and 4B.

claim: No differences in the local expression of various complement regulators were observed in HSV-infected corneas aside from the C1-inhibitor SerpinG1.
source: Likewise, no differences in the local expression of various complement regulators were observed in HSV-infected corneas aside from the C1-inhibitor SerpinG1 (Table 1, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression data shown in Table 1 and Figure 4C.

claim: This expression profile favors local complement activation, as effectors are upregulated without proportional enhancement of pathway regulatory components.
source: Collectively, this expression profile favors local complement activation, as effectors are upregulated without proportional enhancement of pathway regulatory components.
evidence: This is an inference based on the gene expression data showing imbalance between effectors and regulators.

claim: Both tissue-resident non-hematopoietic cells and resident/infiltrating CSF1R+ leukocytes contribute to local C3 expression in the cornea during acute HSV-1 infection.
source: Taken together, our data show that both tissue-resident non-hematopoietic cells and resident/infiltrating CSF1R+ leukocytes contribute to local C3 expression in the cornea during acute HSV-1 infection.
evidence: This is supported by C3 expression analysis in different cell populations shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CVF treatment preserved corneal sensation following HSV-1 infection.
source: Vehicle (PBS)-treated mice exhibited corneal sensation loss following HSV-1 infection, but CVF treatment preserved corneal sensation (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is supported by corneal sensation measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Protein levels of C3 remained near baseline in the cornea following CVF treatment during HSV-1 infection.
source: Protein levels of C3 remained near baseline in the cornea following CVF treatment during HSV-1 infection, yet vehicle-treated animals exhibited a 300–600% increase in C3 protein levels in the cornea at days 3 and 7 p.i. (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by C3 protein measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Ocular CVF treatment did not significantly impact systemic serum C3 concentrations throughout the study.
source: Ocular CVF treatment did not significantly impact systemic serum C3 concentrations throughout the study (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by serum C3 measurements shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Ocular CVF treatment limited corneal edema during HSV-1 infection relative to the vehicle control.
source: Ocular CVF treatment limited corneal edema during HSV-1 infection relative to the vehicle control (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by corneal thickness measurements shown in Figure 5D.

claim: CVF-treated animals had less leukocytic infiltrate (CD45+) into the cornea at day 3 post-infection and, specifically, fewer infiltrating CSF1R+ cells.
source: Consistent with this observation, CVF-treated animals had less leukocytic infiltrate (CD45+) into the cornea at day 3 p.i. and, specifically, fewer infiltrating CSF1R+ cells (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5E and 5F.

claim: By day 7 post-infection, no difference in total CD45+ or CSF1R+ cells were observed in the cornea, yet there was a reduction in the total number of infiltrating CD4+ T cells in CVF-treated animals.
source: By day 7 p.i., no difference in total CD45+ or CSF1R+ cells were observed in the cornea, yet there was a reduction in the total number of infiltrating CD4+ T cells (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: By day 7 post-infection, CVF-treated animals had less virus in the corneas and TG than vehicle controls.
source: By day 7 p.i. CVF-treated animals had less virus in the corneas and TG than vehicle controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that CVF may have unexpected antiviral effects.
evidence: This is supported by viral titer data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: CVF treatment did not have any discernable impact on T cell expansion in the eye-draining MLN or the total number of circulating CXCR3+ CD4+ T cells in HSV-1 infected animals.
source: However, CVF treatment did not have any discernable impact on T cell expansion in the eye-draining MLN or the total number of circulating CXCR3+ CD4+ T cells in HSV-1 infected animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Complement-targeted therapeutics could be tailored for ophthalmic use to limit tissue inflammation and preserve corneal sensation.
source: Collectively, these findings imply that complement-targeted therapeutics could be tailored for ophthalmic use to limit tissue inflammation and preserve corneal sensation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CVF treatment results.

claim: Clinical signs of ocular allergy developed as anticipated in OVA-challenged mice.
source: Clinical signs of ocular allergy developed as anticipated in OVA-challenged mice (Figure 6B), yet corneal sensation loss was not observed (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by clinical scoring data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Corneal sensation loss was not observed in the allergic eye disease (AED) model.
source: Clinical signs of ocular allergy developed as anticipated in OVA-challenged mice (Figure 6B), yet corneal sensation loss was not observed (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is supported by corneal sensation measurements shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Corneas from OVA-challenged mice exhibited CD3+ T cell infiltration by challenge day 7.
source: Consistent with development of AED, corneas from OVA-challenged mice exhibited CD3+ T cell infiltration by challenge day 7 (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Frank corneal nerve loss was not observed in AED.
source: However, frank corneal nerve loss was not observed in AED (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Morphometric analysis confirmed the preservation of corneal nerve density during AED.
source: Morphometric analysis of confocal image stacks confirmed the preservation of corneal nerve density during AED (Figure 6E), although CD3+ T cell numbers were elevated in sensitized animals relative to healthy controls (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figures 6E and 6F.

claim: The cornea-infiltrating T cells were predominately CD4+ in the AED model.
source: Flow cytometry was used to verify that the cornea-infiltrating T cells were predominately CD4+ in the AED model (Figure 6G).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Progressive corneal sensation loss was observed following transfer of CD4+ T cells with and without addition of CD8+ T cells in the GVHD model.
source: Progressive corneal sensation loss was observed following transfer of CD4+ T cells with and without addition of CD8+ T cells. Addition of CD8+ T cells alone evoked a transient corneal sensation deficit that recovered by day 26 post-transplant. However, corneal sensation loss was not observed in the BM only control group (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by corneal sensation measurements shown in Figure 7B.

claim: External signs of ocular disease were apparent in groups receiving CD4+ T cells by the study endpoint in the GVHD model.
source: External signs of ocular disease (see Table 2) were also apparent in groups receiving CD4+ T cells by the study endpoint (Figure 7C).
evidence: This is supported by external photographs shown in Figure 7C and scoring criteria in Table 2.

claim: Corneal nerve integrity was markedly reduced in groups receiving CD4+ T cells in the GVHD model.
source: Consistent with sensation loss, corneal nerve integrity was markedly reduced in groups receiving CD4+ T cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Morphometric analysis confirmed the CD4-dependent decrease in corneal nerve density in the GVHD model.
source: Morphometric analysis of confocal image stacks confirmed the CD4-dependent decrease in corneal nerve density (Figure 7E) and concomitant increase in total CD3+ cells (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figures 7E and 7F.

claim: Corneal sensation loss occurs early in ocular GVHD and this pathology is instigated in part by allogeneic CD4+ T cells.
source: Taken together, our data show for the first time that corneal sensation loss occurs early in ocular GVHD and that this pathology is instigated in part by allogeneic CD4+ T cells.
evidence: This is a novel finding from the GVHD experiments presented in the manuscript.

claim: Systemic disease progressed equally in both GVHD cohorts regardless of CVF or PBS treatment.
source: Systemic disease progressed equally in both GVHD cohorts regardless of treatment (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by systemic disease scores shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Systemic serum C3 concentrations were lower in the GVHD cohort treated with CVF compared to the PBS-treated GVHD groups at the study endpoint.
source: Although CVF administration was limited to the eye, systemic serum C3 concentrations were lower in the GVHD cohort treated with CVF compared to the PBS-treated GVHD groups at the study endpoint.
evidence: This is supported by serum C3 measurements shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The inverted CD4:CD8 T cell ratio in the spleens and eye-draining mandibular lymph nodes of both groups of GVHD mice confirmed the presence of systemic disease.
source: Nonetheless, the inverted CD4:CD8 T cell ratio (Herretes et al., 2015) in the spleens and eye-draining mandibular lymph nodes of both groups of GVHD mice confirmed the presence of systemic disease (Figure 8D).
evidence: This is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 8D and a citation to Herretes et al., 2015.

claim: Local CVF treatment preserved corneal nerve integrity and mechano-sensory function in ocular GVHD despite development of systemic disease.
source: Despite development of systemic disease, local CVF treatment preserved corneal nerve integrity and mechano-sensory function in ocular GVHD (Figure 8E,F).
evidence: This is supported by corneal sensation measurements and confocal microscopy images shown in Figures 8E and 8F.

claim: Morphometric analysis corroborated the preservation of corneal nerve density in CVF-treated mice from the GVHD cohort.
source: Morphometric analysis of confocal image stacks from the study endpoint corroborated the preservation of corneal nerve density in CVF-treated mice from the GVHD cohort (Figure 8G), although CVF did not reduce the number of total CD3+ cells during GVHD relative to PBS (Figure 8H).
evidence: This is supported by morphometric analysis shown in Figures 8G and 8H.

claim: CVF treatment limited GVHD-associated periocular disease in female but not in male mice.
source: In addition, CVF treatment also limited GVHD-associated periocular disease in female but not in male mice (Figure 8—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by ophthalmic disease scores shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: CD4+ T cells and complement C3 coordinate corneal sensory nerve damage in both herpetic keratitis and ocular GVHD.
source: In summary, these preclinical models establish that CD4+ T cells and complement C3 coordinate corneal sensory nerve damage in both herpetic keratitis and ocular GHVD.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from both HSV-1 and GVHD models.

claim: Complement-targeted therapeutics may limit the severity of immune-mediated sensory nerve damage at the ocular surface.
source: Moreover, our data provide a proof of principle that complement-targeted therapeutics may limit the severity of immune-mediated sensory nerve damage at the ocular surface.
evidence: This is based on the CVF treatment results in both HSV-1 and GVHD models.

claim: Ocular HSV-1 infection provokes corneal denervation and sensation loss between days 5 to 8 post-infection in immunologically naive C57BL/6 mice.
source: Ocular HSV-1 infection provokes corneal denervation and sensation loss between days 5 to 8 post-infection (p.i.) in immunologically naive C57BL/6 mice (Chucair-Elliott et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chucair-Elliott et al., 2015.

claim: The tempo of HSV-associated sensation loss appears to be synchronized with the host transition from innate to adaptive immunity following infection.
source: This tempo appears to be synchronized with the host transition from innate to adaptive immunity following infection.
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of sensation loss and T cell infiltration.

claim: Local complement activation and T cell engagement coordinate corneal nerve damage during HSV-1 infection.
source: Accordingly, we hypothesized that local complement activation and T cell engagement coordinate corneal nerve damage during HSV-1 infection.
evidence: This is the central hypothesis tested in the manuscript.

claim: Adaptive immunity prevents recovery of corneal sensory function following ocular HSV-1 infection.
source: Adaptive immunity has been shown to prevent recovery of corneal sensory function following ocular HSV-1 infection (Yun et al., 2014), but the initial pathophysiological triggers of denervation and sensation loss are not definitively characterized.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Yun et al., 2014.

claim: The initial pathophysiological triggers of denervation and sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis are not definitively characterized.
source: Adaptive immunity has been shown to prevent recovery of corneal sensory function following ocular HSV-1 infection (Yun et al., 2014), but the initial pathophysiological triggers of denervation and sensation loss are not definitively characterized.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: The divergence in corneal sensation between WT and C3-/- mice does not stem from differential susceptibility to HSV-1 infection.
source: Viral titers were measured at time points before and after the onset of corneal sensation loss to determine whether the divergence in sensation stemmed from a differential susceptibility to infection. On day 3 p.i., the HSV-1 burden was similar in the tear film, corneas, and TG of WT and C3-/- animals (Figure 1C–D).
evidence: Similar viral titers at day 3 p.i. indicate that differential susceptibility to infection is not the cause of sensation differences.

claim: C3-deficiency does not impair T cell priming, clonal expansion, or recruitment to the cornea during HSV-1 infection.
source: Although T cells successfully extravasate into the corneas of WT and C3-/- mice (Figure 1F,G), C3-deficiency can have broad impacts on T cell priming, clonal expansion, and recruitment (Clarke and Tenner, 2014; West et al., 2018). To investigate this possibility, corneas from HSV-1-infected WT and C3-/- mice were evaluated for chemokines associated with T cell recruitment, and the eye-draining mandibular lymph nodes (MLN) were harvested to evaluate T cell responses.
evidence: The experiments in Figure 2 were designed to test whether C3-deficiency affects T cell responses, and the results showed no impairment.

claim: C3 is not required for T cell expansion and functional responses during HSV-1 infection.
source: Chemokines associated with T cell recruitment were elevated in corneas from both WT and C3-/- mice at day 5 p.i.—a time consistent with onset of sensation loss (Figure 2A). Moreover, CD4+ and CD8+ T cell expansion was comparable within the eye-draining mandibular lymph nodes (MLN) from WT and C3-/- mice (Figure 2B). Similarly, T cells harvested from WT and C3-/- mice at day 8 p.i. responded equally to in vitro stimulation in terms of IFNγ production (Figure 2C).
evidence: The data in Figures 2A-C collectively show that C3 is not required for T cell expansion and function.

claim: Both C3 and T cells are required for corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection.
source: In support of our hypothesis that C3 and T cells jointly coordinate corneal sensation loss, frank corneal sensation loss was not observed following ocular HSV-1 infection in C3-sufficient, alpha-beta T cell receptor-deficient mice (TCRα-/-) which congenitally lack classical CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: The absence of sensation loss in TCRα-/- mice (which have C3 but no T cells) combined with the absence of sensation loss in C3-/- mice (which have T cells but no C3) demonstrates that both are required.

claim: C3-/- T cells do not have functional defects in mediating corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection.
source: To investigate potential functional defects of C3-/- T cells in an in vivo context, CD3+ T cells were harvested from HSV-infected WT or C3-/- mice at day 8 p.i. and adoptively transferred into TCRα-/- mice. Six days following cell transfer, TCRα-/- recipients were infected with HSV-1 and corneal sensation monitored longitudinally. Adoptive transfer of CD3+ T cells from either WT or C3-/- donors evoked progressive corneal sensation loss in TCRα-/- recipients by day 8 p.i. (Figure 2D).
evidence: The ability of C3-/- T cells to induce sensation loss when transferred into TCRα-/- mice (which have C3) demonstrates that C3-/- T cells are functionally competent.

claim: CD8+ T cells are not sufficient to drive corneal sensation loss during acute HSV-1 infection.
source: Our data show that T cells contribute to corneal sensation loss during acute HSV-1 infection, yet whether this pathology is dependent upon CD4+ or CD8+ T cells remained unclear. To better discern the contributions of each subset, CD4+ and CD8+ T cells were harvested from infected WT mice, transferred into separate groups of TCRα-/- mice, and recipient mice subsequently infected with HSV-1. Corneal sensation loss during acute HSV-1 infection was only observed upon reconstitution with CD4+ T cells (Figure 3A).
evidence: The adoptive transfer experiments show that only CD4+ T cells, not CD8+ T cells, are sufficient to drive sensation loss.

claim: Antigen specificity is required for CD4+ T cells to mediate corneal sensation loss during HSV-1 infection.
source: The requirement for antigen specificity was subsequently evaluated during acute HSV-1 infection by monitoring corneal sensation in WT and OT-II transgenic mice that generate ovalbumin (OVA)-specific CD4 T cells. Transgenic OT-II mice did not exhibit corneal sensation loss following infection despite evidence of bystander CD4+ T cell activation and recruitment into the cornea (Figure 3B–D).
evidence: OT-II mice with OVA-specific CD4+ T cells did not develop sensation loss during HSV-1 infection, indicating that HSV-1-specific CD4+ T cells are required.

claim: Active HSV-1 infection is required for CD4+ T cell-mediated corneal sensation loss.
source: Abrasion of the corneal epithelium, which is required to mediate infection in this model, induces local chemokine expression capable of recruiting T cells to the cornea even in the absence of viral infection (Liu et al., 2012). Nonetheless, active corneal HSV-1 infection was necessary to provoke corneal sensation loss, as TCRα-/- mice reconstituted with CD4+ T cells harvested from HSV-infected WT mice did not elicit auto/allo-antigen-associated sensation loss within two weeks of corneal scratch injury (i.e. mock infection) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Mock infection experiments show that corneal injury alone is not sufficient; active HSV-1 infection is required.

claim: Monocytes and tissue macrophages are sources of C3.
source: Monocytes and tissue macrophages are known sources of C3 (Einstein et al., 1977; Lubbers et al., 2017; Morgan and Gasque, 1997; Verschoor et al., 2001), thus CSF1R+ cells from the peripheral blood of transgenic CSF1R-GFP mice (MAFIA) were utilized as the relative standard for C3 transcript expression.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: C3 expression was detected in CD45+ leukocytes isolated from HSV-1 infected corneas.
source: Expression of C3 was noted in CD45+ leukocytes isolated from infected corneas, yet detection of C3 expression was lost when CSF1R+ cells were removed from the total CD45+ pool.
evidence: This is supported by C3 expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: CSF1R+ cells are the primary leukocyte source of C3 in HSV-1 infected corneas.
source: Expression of C3 was noted in CD45+ leukocytes isolated from infected corneas, yet detection of C3 expression was lost when CSF1R+ cells were removed from the total CD45+ pool.
evidence: The loss of C3 expression when CSF1R+ cells are removed indicates they are the primary leukocyte source.

claim: Isolated EpCAM+ corneal epithelial cells expressed C3 at levels comparable to blood monocytes during HSV-1 infection.
source: In addition, isolated EpCAM+ corneal epithelial cells expressed C3 at levels comparable to blood monocytes.
evidence: This is supported by C3 expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The C3 expression level was greater in whole-cornea preparations than among individual cell fractions during HSV-1 infection.
source: However, the C3 expression level was greater in whole-cornea preparations than among individual cell fractions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by C3 expression analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Multiple cell types in the cornea contribute to local C3 production during HSV-1 infection.
source: However, the C3 expression level was greater in whole-cornea preparations than among individual cell fractions (Figure 4D). Taken together, our data show that both tissue-resident non-hematopoietic cells and resident/infiltrating CSF1R+ leukocytes contribute to local C3 expression in the cornea during acute HSV-1 infection.
evidence: The higher C3 expression in whole cornea compared to individual fractions suggests multiple cell types contribute.

claim: Local control of complement activation can be harnessed to prevent corneal nerve damage during HSV-1 infection.
source: Ocular HSV-1 infection amplifies local complement gene expression, yet whether local control of complement activation can be harnessed to prevent corneal nerve damage has not been explored. From a clinical perspective, modulating complement activation at the ocular surface may be a viable therapeutic option. As a proof of concept, daily ocular cobra venom factor (CVF) treatment was explored as a putative method to deplete C3 and preserve corneal sensation during acute HSV-1 infection.
evidence: The CVF treatment experiments demonstrate that local complement control can prevent nerve damage.

claim: Modulating complement activation at the ocular surface may be a viable therapeutic option for HSV-1 keratitis.
source: From a clinical perspective, modulating complement activation at the ocular surface may be a viable therapeutic option.
evidence: This is based on the successful CVF treatment results.

claim: CVF treatment depletes C3 in the cornea during HSV-1 infection.
source: Protein levels of C3 remained near baseline in the cornea following CVF treatment during HSV-1 infection, yet vehicle-treated animals exhibited a 300–600% increase in C3 protein levels in the cornea at days 3 and 7 p.i. (Figure 5B).
evidence: The maintenance of baseline C3 levels in CVF-treated corneas while vehicle-treated corneas show increased C3 demonstrates effective C3 depletion.

claim: CVF treatment has localized effects on complement depletion when administered topically to the eye.
source: Ocular CVF treatment did not significantly impact systemic serum C3 concentrations throughout the study (Figure 5C).
evidence: The lack of effect on systemic C3 levels indicates localized action of topical CVF treatment.

claim: CVF treatment reduces inflammation in the cornea during HSV-1 infection.
source: Ocular CVF treatment limited corneal edema during HSV-1 infection relative to the vehicle control (Figure 5D). Consistent with this observation, CVF-treated animals had less leukocytic infiltrate (CD45+) into the cornea at day 3 p.i. and, specifically, fewer infiltrating CSF1R+ cells (Figure 5E,F).
evidence: Reduced corneal edema and leukocyte infiltration indicate decreased inflammation.

claim: CVF may have antiviral effects during HSV-1 infection.
source: By day 7 p.i. CVF-treated animals had less virus in the corneas and TG than vehicle controls (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), suggesting that CVF may have unexpected antiviral effects.
evidence: The reduced viral titers in CVF-treated animals suggest possible antiviral effects, though this is speculative.

claim: The pathobiology underlying non-penetrating corneal nerve damage is not well understood.
source: The pathobiology underlying non-penetrating corneal nerve damage is not well understood, although inflammation is generally recognized as an important feature (Neelam et al., 2018; Shaheen et al., 2014; Cruzat et al., 2015; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2016; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017a).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Inflammation is generally recognized as an important feature of non-penetrating corneal nerve damage.
source: The pathobiology underlying non-penetrating corneal nerve damage is not well understood, although inflammation is generally recognized as an important feature (Neelam et al., 2018; Shaheen et al., 2014; Cruzat et al., 2015; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2016; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A variety of pathogenic microbes impair the corneal nerve architecture upon ocular infection.
source: While HSV-1 is a clinically prominent cause of corneal nerve damage and sensation loss, a variety of pathogenic microbes impair the corneal nerve architecture upon ocular infection (Cruzat et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Cruzat et al., 2015.

claim: The neurotropism of HSV-1 is not directly responsible for corneal nerve damage.
source: This observation adds to evidence that the neurotropism of HSV-1 is not directly responsible for nerve damage (Chucair-Elliott et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Chucair-Elliott et al., 2016.

claim: Corneal nerve alterations in dry eye disease are associated with a broad array of neuropathic clinical symptoms including dryness, itch, and pain.
source: In addition to sensation loss evoked by HSV-1, corneal nerve alterations in other contexts such as dry eye disease are associated with a broad array of neuropathic clinical symptoms including dryness, itch, and pain (Andersen et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Andersen et al., 2017.

claim: Complement has been implicated in the etiology of systemic GVHD and allergic inflammation.
source: Our rationale for this is that complement has been implicated in the etiology of systemic GVHD and allergic inflammation (Gour et al., 2018; Kwan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Nguyen et al., 2018; Zhang and Köhl, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: A neuroinflammatory role of complement has not been described for GVHD or allergic inflammation within the eye.
source: However, a neuroinflammatory role of complement has not been described for either disease within the eye.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: Architectural changes in the corneal nerves occur in patients with herpetic keratitis, chronic ocular allergy, and ocular GVHD.
source: The translational relevance of this study is underscored by in vivo confocal microscopy data from multiple clinical studies showing architectural changes in the corneal nerves of patients with herpetic keratitis, chronic ocular allergy, and ocular GVHD (Hamrah et al., 2010; Müller et al., 2015; Moein et al., 2018; Hu et al., 2008; Le et al., 2011; Leonardi et al., 2012; Tepelus et al., 2017; He et al., 2017a).
evidence: This is supported by multiple clinical study citations.

claim: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is a common cause of neurotropic keratitis and remains a leading cause of infectious corneal blindness.
source: Herpes simplex virus type 1 (HSV-1) is a common cause of neurotropic keratitis and remains a leading cause of infectious corneal blindness (Sacchetti and Lambiase, 2014; Farooq and Shukla, 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Sacchetti and Lambiase, 2014 and Farooq and Shukla, 2012.

claim: The incidence of ocular allergy exceeds twenty percent of the population.
source: The incidence of ocular allergy exceeds twenty percent of the population with varying degrees of neurogenic ocular surface discomfort that can severely diminish quality of life (Craig et al., 2017; Patel et al., 2017; Saban et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: GVHD is the greatest cause of non-relapse morbidity following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT).
source: Finally, GVHD is the greatest cause of non-relapse morbidity following hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (HSCT) used to treat life-threatening malignancies and immunologic diseases (MacDonald et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to MacDonald et al., 2017.

claim: A majority of patients with chronic presentations of GVHD suffer from ocular surface involvement.
source: A majority of patients with chronic presentations of GVHD suffer from ocular surface involvement (Shikari et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Shikari et al., 2013.

claim: Allergy symptoms were not accompanied by frank loss of corneal mechano-sensation in the AED animal model.
source: Although clinical data show that corneal nerve remodeling can occur in patients with chronic ocular allergy (Hu et al., 2008; Le et al., 2011), allergy symptoms were not accompanied by frank loss of corneal mechano-sensation in the AED animal model.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the AED model shown in Figure 6.

claim: Corneal nerve remodeling can occur in patients with chronic ocular allergy.
source: Although clinical data show that corneal nerve remodeling can occur in patients with chronic ocular allergy (Hu et al., 2008; Le et al., 2011), allergy symptoms were not accompanied by frank loss of corneal mechano-sensation in the AED animal model.
evidence: This is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2008 and Le et al., 2011.

claim: The AED model shows that T cell infiltration alone is not sufficient to cause corneal sensation loss.
source: Consistent with development of AED, corneas from OVA-challenged mice exhibited CD3+ T cell infiltration by challenge day 7 (Figure 6D). However, frank corneal nerve loss was not observed in AED (Figure 6D).
evidence: The presence of T cell infiltration without sensation loss in AED demonstrates that T cells alone are not sufficient.

claim: The inflammatory neuroimmune pathology involving C3 and CD4+ T cells is context-dependent.
source: However, this was not the case in a T-dependent allergic eye disease (AED) model, suggesting that this inflammatory neuroimmune pathology is specific to certain disease etiologies.
evidence: The differential outcomes in AED versus HSV-1 and GVHD models demonstrate context-dependency.

claim: AED is driven primarily by a combined Th2/Th17 CD4 T cell response.
source: Furthermore, AED is driven primarily by a combined Th2/Th17 CD4 T cell response that differs from the Th1 bias observed in HSV-1 keratitis and ocular GVHD (Herretes et al., 2015; Saban et al., 2013; Tang and Hendricks, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: HSV-1 keratitis and ocular GVHD are characterized by a Th1 bias.
source: Furthermore, AED is driven primarily by a combined Th2/Th17 CD4 T cell response that differs from the Th1 bias observed in HSV-1 keratitis and ocular GVHD (Herretes et al., 2015; Saban et al., 2013; Tang and Hendricks, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Th1 cytokines such as IFNγ, IL-2, and lymphotoxin-alpha may be important in coordinating corneal sensation loss.
source: This suggests that Th1 cytokines such as IFNγ, IL-2, and lymphotoxin-alpha may be important in coordinating corneal sensation loss.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the differential T cell polarization patterns.

claim: The unique inflammatory milieus and differential polarizations of cornea-infiltrating T cells across disease models may influence the downstream effects of complement activation.
source: Nonetheless, the unique inflammatory milieus and differential polarizations of cornea-infiltrating T cells across these disease models may also influence the downstream effects of complement activation in the tissue microenvironment (Tomlinson and Thurman, 2018).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to Tomlinson and Thurman, 2018.

claim: Complement enhances clearance of infected cells and nascent virions during HSV-1 infection.
source: Complement enhances clearance of infected cells and nascent virions during HSV-1 infection (Kostavasili et al., 1997; Lubinski et al., 2002; McNearney et al., 1987).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: HSV-1 can evade C3 activation through endogenous expression of glycoprotein C (gC).
source: Importantly, HSV-1 can also evade C3 activation through endogenous expression of glycoprotein C (gC). By limiting C3b deposition on infected cells and nascent virions, gC can inhibit subsequent C5 binding and membrane attack complex (MAC) formation (Kostavasili et al., 1997; Lubinski et al., 2002; McNearney et al., 1987; Tegla et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Herpetic keratitis is less severe in rabbits infected with a gC-deficient strain of HSV-1 during acute infection.
source: This could explain why herpetic keratitis is less severe in rabbits infected with a gC-deficient strain of HSV-1 during acute infection (Drolet et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Drolet et al., 2004.

claim: gC-mediated viral evasion strategy may be cell type-dependent.
source: However, this gC-mediated viral evasion strategy may also be cell type-dependent.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the following evidence about differential responses in different cell types.

claim: Neuronal cells maintain host-encoded complement regulator expression more efficiently and are more resistant to MAC deposition than epithelial cells upon HSV-1 infection.
source: Cell culture modeling indicates that neuronal cells maintain host-encoded complement regulator expression more efficiently and are more resistant to MAC deposition than epithelial cells upon HSV-1 infection (Rautemaa et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Rautemaa et al., 2002.

claim: Complement-mediated sensory nerve damage in HSV-1 keratitis may reflect a maladaptive outcome of host-defense.
source: Accordingly, complement-mediated sensory nerve damage in HSV-1 keratitis may reflect a maladaptive outcome of host-defense.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the evidence that complement is involved in both viral clearance and nerve damage.

claim: The maintenance of corneal innervation in C3-/- mice enables enhanced shedding of nascent virions produced within the TG.
source: The absence of a concordant difference in HSV-1 titers in corneas from WT and C3-/- mice is likely explained by the potent antiviral effects of type-1 interferon (Conrady et al., 2011; Royer and Carr, 2016). This suggests that the maintenance of corneal innervation in C3-/- mice enables enhanced shedding of nascent virions produced within the TG.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of increased viral shedding in C3-/- mice with intact innervation.

claim: There is no difference in the amount of latent HSV-1 in the TG of naive WT and C3-/- mice 30 days after ocular HSV-1 challenge.
source: Moreover, there is no difference in the amount of latent HSV-1 in the TG of naive WT and C3-/- mice 30 days after ocular HSV-1 challenge (Royer et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2019.

claim: C3 is involved in progression of keratitis and sensory nerve fiber retraction during acute HSV-1 infection but likely does not contribute to complete elimination of infected nerves.
source: Taken together, this evidence indicates that although C3 is involved in progression of keratitis and sensory nerve fiber retraction during acute infection, it likely does not contribute to complete elimination of infected nerves.
evidence: This is an inference based on the collective findings about C3's role in nerve damage but not viral latency.

claim: The impacts of preexisting humoral immune responses on complement pathway activation and regulation in the cornea during HSV-1 infection remain incompletely understood.
source: The studies reported herein involve immunologically naive mice, but the impacts of preexisting humoral immune responses on complement pathway activation and regulation in the cornea during HSV-1 infection remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This identifies a limitation of the current study and a knowledge gap.

claim: Herpes-associated neurotropic keratitis typically develops as a result of recurrent corneal infections in patients.
source: This point is of considerable importance clinically, as herpes-associated neurotropic keratitis typically develops as a result of recurrent corneal infections in patients (Hamrah et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Hamrah et al., 2010.

claim: C3 is essential for optimal antibody-dependent viral clearance following ocular HSV-1 challenge in mice.
source: Furthermore, we have recently reported that C3 is essential for optimal antibody-dependent viral clearance following ocular HSV-1 challenge in mice (Royer et al., 2019; Royer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Royer et al., 2019 and Royer et al., 2017.

claim: Vaccinated animals did not exhibit corneal sensation loss following ocular HSV-1 infection.
source: While vaccinated animals did not exhibit corneal sensation loss following ocular HSV-1 infection in those studies, deposition of the terminal C3 cleavage product C3d was present in the corneal epithelium (Royer et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Royer et al., 2017.

claim: HSV-1 infection creates an imbalance in the local complement effector to regulator expression ratios that contribute to aberrant complement pathway activation in the cornea.
source: Host gene expression data herein corroborates that HSV-1 infection creates an imbalance in the local complement effector to regulator expression ratios that contribute to aberrant complement pathway activation in the cornea.
evidence: This is supported by the gene expression data shown in Figures 4A-C and Table 1.

claim: This imbalance in 'complement proteostasis' may favor deposition of complement fragments and sublytic MAC on corneal sensory nerve fibers.
source: This imbalance in 'complement proteostasis' may favor deposition of complement fragments and sublytic MAC on corneal sensory nerve fibers (Tegla et al., 2011; Triantafilou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to Tegla et al., 2011 and Triantafilou et al., 2013.

claim: The nerve-intrinsic molecular mechanisms responsible for trigeminal sensory fiber retraction, neuronal death, or axonal regeneration in the cornea are largely unknown.
source: Notwithstanding, the nerve-intrinsic molecular mechanisms responsible for trigeminal sensory fiber retraction, neuronal death, or axonal regeneration in the cornea are largely unknown (Stepp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stepp et al., 2017 and identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Identification of the complement pathway's role in initiating corneal sensation loss following HSV-1 infection introduces an array of potential drug targets for local therapy.
source: Identification of the complement pathway's role in initiating corneal sensation loss following HSV-1 infection is an important advancement in the mechanistic understanding of this disease process, as it introduces an array of potential drug targets for local therapy.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings of the study.

claim: Complement activation in antigen-induced keratitis may be mediated by cellular immune mechanisms.
source: Previous observations note that complement activation in antigen-induced keratitis may be mediated by cellular immune mechanisms (Verhagen et al., 1992).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Verhagen et al., 1992.

claim: CSF1R+ macrophages/monocytes are recruited to the cornea in the early stages of HSV-1 infection and are associated with corneal nerve damage.
source: The identification of CSF1R+ macrophages/monocytes as a local source of C3 during infection (Figure 4D) is also critical, as these cells are recruited to the cornea in the early stages of HSV-1 infection and are associated with corneal nerve damage in HSV-1 keratitis (Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b; Conrady et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b and Conrady et al., 2013.

claim: CD4 T cells coordinate corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis.
source: Moreover, CD4 T cells coordinate this pathology. Our data corroborate findings from the Hendricks' lab showing that CD4 T cells are associated with corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis (Yun et al., 2014), yet our adoptive transfer experiments establish that this process is not dependent upon endogenous C3 production by cornea-infiltrating donor T cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and a citation to Yun et al., 2014.

claim: Corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis is not dependent upon endogenous C3 production by cornea-infiltrating T cells.
source: Our data corroborate findings from the Hendricks' lab showing that CD4 T cells are associated with corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 keratitis (Yun et al., 2014), yet our adoptive transfer experiments establish that this process is not dependent upon endogenous C3 production by cornea-infiltrating donor T cells (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is supported by adoptive transfer experiments showing C3-/- T cells can induce sensation loss in C3-sufficient recipients.

claim: The tempo of HSV-associated sensation loss was consistent among models once initiated.
source: Notably, the tempo of HSV-associated sensation loss was consistent among models once initiated (Figure 1B, Figure 2D, Figure 3A).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of sensation loss kinetics across different experimental models.

claim: The initial onset of sensation loss was delayed by one day in the adoptive transfer model compared to WT mice.
source: However, the initial onset was delayed by one day in the adoptive transfer model. This likely reflects the relative lymphopenic status of T cell-reconstituted TCRα-/- mice compared to WT mice (compare Figure 2B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of T cell numbers in different experimental groups.

claim: Corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 infection and ocular GVHD share a common mechanism dependent upon CD4+ T cells and complement C3.
source: Corneal sensation loss in HSV-1 infection and ocular GVHD shared a common mechanism dependent upon CD4+ T cells and complement C3.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings from both disease models.

claim: The role of intracellular C3 in regulating human Th1 responses has received much attention in recent years.
source: The role of intracellular C3 in regulating human Th1 responses has received much attention in recent years (Elvington et al., 2017; Hansen et al., 2019; Liszewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mice do not express CD46.
source: However, mice do not express CD46.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about species differences in complement regulation.

claim: Anaphylatoxin receptor signaling has been shown to modulate Th1 cytokine production in murine T cells.
source: Instead, anaphylatoxin receptor signaling has been shown to modulate Th1 cytokine production in murine T cells (Strainic et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Strainic et al., 2008.

claim: There is no defect in IFNγ production by CD4 T cells from C3-/- mice following HSV-1 infection.
source: Our ex vivo re-stimulation data clearly show that there is no defect in IFNγ production by CD4 T cells from C3-/- mice following HSV-1 infection.
evidence: This is supported by the in vitro stimulation data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: T cell proliferation in response to re-stimulation with HSV-1 antigen is similar in WT and C3-/- mice.
source: Others have shown similar data based on T cell proliferation in response to re-stimulation with HSV-1 antigen (Da Costa et al., 1999).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Da Costa et al., 1999.

claim: A reduction in IFNγ production by CD4 T cells from C3-/- mice was reported following in vitro expansion under Th1 polarizing conditions.
source: In contrast, a reduction in IFNγ production by CD4 T cells from C3-/- mice was reported following in vitro expansion under Th1 polarizing conditions (Liszewski et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Liszewski et al., 2013.

claim: Anaphylatoxin receptor signaling from locally produced C3a and potentially C5a may modulate T cell effector function upon extravasation into the inflamed cornea.
source: Nonetheless, it is possible that anaphylatoxin receptor signaling from locally produced C3a (and potentially C5a generated downstream) modulates T cell effector function upon extravasation into the inflamed cornea.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential mechanisms.

claim: The precise relationships between T cells and C3 in mouse models of corneal neuropathic disease remain to be identified.
source: The precise relationships between T cells and C3 in our mouse models of corneal neuropathic disease remain to be identified.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction.

claim: The working hypothesis involves an indirect mechanism whereby sublytic MAC deposition from local complement activation damages sensory nerves, which are then cleared by T cell-activated phagocytes or other cytolytic cells.
source: Our working hypothesis involves an indirect mechanism whereby sublytic MAC deposition from local complement activation damages sensory nerves, which are then cleared by T cell-activated phagocytes or other cytolytic cells.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanistic model based on the findings.

claim: Tissue-resident and infiltrating leukocytes as well as nerve-associated corneal epithelial cells could be involved in clearing damaged nerves.
source: These could include tissue-resident and infiltrating leukocytes (macrophages, monocytes, dendritic cells, and NK cells) as well as nerve-associated corneal epithelial cells (Buela and Hendricks, 2015; Chucair-Elliott et al., 2017b; Gao et al., 2016a; Koyama and Hill, 2016; Liu et al., 2017; Royer et al., 2018; Seyed-Razavi et al., 2014; Stepp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The plasma membranes of corneal nerves and epithelial cells fuse thereby enabling cytosolic exchange.
source: Emerging evidence indicates that the plasma membranes of corneal nerves and epithelial cells fuse thereby enabling cytosolic exchange (Stepp et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Stepp et al., 2017.

claim: Complement-mediated damage to corneal epithelial cells may have a direct impact on sensory nerves.
source: In light of this, it is plausible that complement-mediated damage to corneal epithelial cells has a direct impact on sensory nerves.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the evidence of membrane fusion between nerves and epithelial cells.

claim: This is the first report documenting loss of corneal mechano-sensory function in ocular GVHD.
source: Although corneal nerve damage is an established pathology in animal models of HSV-1 infection (Chucair-Elliott et al., 2015; He et al., 2017b; Yun et al., 2014), this is the first report documenting loss of corneal mechano-sensory function in ocular GVHD.
evidence: This is a novel finding of the study.

claim: Patients rarely exhibit neurological manifestations of GVHD affecting other tissues/organs.
source: Notably, patients rarely exhibit neurological manifestations of GVHD affecting other tissues/organs (Grauer et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Grauer et al., 2010.

claim: Corneal sensation loss may provide a clinical benchmark for initiation of targeted therapies to curb progression of ocular GVHD in patients.
source: Corneal sensation loss may provide a clinical benchmark for initiation of targeted therapies to curb progression of ocular GVHD in patients.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical applications.

claim: Corneal sensation loss is an early warning sign of progressive ocular and systemic GVHD in the animal model.
source: Data from our animal model of GVHD suggest that corneal sensation loss is an early warning sign of progressive ocular and systemic GVHD.
evidence: This is supported by the GVHD experimental data showing early sensation loss.

claim: Corneal sensation measurements are warranted in patients following HSCT to substantiate the finding that sensation loss is an early sign of GVHD.
source: Corneal sensation measurements are warranted in patients following HSCT to substantiate this finding among those who develop chronic GVHD.
evidence: This is a recommendation for future clinical studies.

claim: Corneal nerve remodeling occurs in patients with ocular GVHD.
source: Published imaging studies confirm that corneal nerve remodeling occurs in patients with ocular GVHD (He et al., 2017a; Tepelus et al., 2017); therefore, clinical studies to delineate the kinetics of disease onset are needed.
evidence: This is supported by citations to He et al., 2017a and Tepelus et al., 2017.

claim: Complement C3 is a known driver of systemic GVHD.
source: Complement C3 is a known driver of systemic GVHD (Kwan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Seignez et al., 2017), and our data show that aberrant complement pathway activation also contributes to the pathogenesis of ocular GVHD including corneal sensation loss.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Aberrant complement pathway activation contributes to the pathogenesis of ocular GVHD including corneal sensation loss.
source: Complement C3 is a known driver of systemic GVHD (Kwan et al., 2012; Ma et al., 2014; Seignez et al., 2017), and our data show that aberrant complement pathway activation also contributes to the pathogenesis of ocular GVHD including corneal sensation loss.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from the GVHD model.

claim: Localized CVF treatment preserved corneal sensation in both sexes during ocular GVHD.
source: Furthermore, localized CVF treatment preserved corneal sensation in both sexes during ocular GVHD, but treatment only abrogated other facets of ocular surface disease in female mice.
evidence: This is supported by the CVF treatment data in the GVHD model shown in Figure 8.

claim: CVF treatment only abrogated other facets of ocular surface disease in female mice during GVHD.
source: Furthermore, localized CVF treatment preserved corneal sensation in both sexes during ocular GVHD, but treatment only abrogated other facets of ocular surface disease in female mice.
evidence: This is supported by the sex-stratified analysis shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: The dimorphic outcome of CVF treatment in GVHD may reflect insufficient maintenance of C3 depletion in the ocular surface microenvironment.
source: This dimorphic outcome may reflect insufficient maintenance of C3 depletion in the ocular surface microenvironment, as animals were only treated twice weekly.
evidence: This is a speculation about the cause of sex differences in treatment response.

claim: Complement activity is reportedly limited by terminal pathway components in female mice compared to males.
source: Furthermore, complement activity is reportedly limited by terminal pathway components in female mice compared to males (Kotimaa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kotimaa et al., 2016.

claim: Sensory nerve involvement may be a unique facet and treatment target in ocular GVHD.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that sensory nerve involvement may be a unique facet and treatment target in ocular GVHD.
evidence: This is an inference based on the findings that corneal sensation loss occurs in ocular GVHD and can be prevented by complement inhibition.

claim: C3 is the heart of the complement pathway and its activation products mediate virtually all downstream pathway functions.
source: While the complement pathway has many components, C3 is the heart of the pathway and its activation products mediate virtually all downstream pathway functions.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about the complement cascade.

claim: CVF was used to target complement activation as a proof of concept for local delivery of complement-targeted therapeutics for ocular surface disease.
source: Accordingly, we used CVF to target complement activation in models of HSV-1 keratitis and ocular GVHD as a proof of concept for local delivery of complement-targeted therapeutics for ocular surface disease.
evidence: This describes the rationale for using CVF in the study.

claim: Purified CVF is a 'nontoxic' derivative in contrast to the neurotoxic effects of complete cobra venom.
source: In contrast to the neurotoxic effects of complete cobra venom, purified CVF is a 'nontoxic' derivative.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about CVF.

claim: CVF forms a biochemically stable convertase to rapidly hydrolyze mammalian C3 and C5, resulting in complement inactivation via effector consumption.
source: CVF forms a biochemically stable convertase to rapidly hydrolyze mammalian C3 and C5. This ultimately results in complement inactivation via effector consumption (Vogel and Fritzinger, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Vogel and Fritzinger, 2010.

claim: The only recorded side effect of purified CVF administration in rodents is transitory anaphylatoxin-mediated pulmonary inflammation resulting in acute respiratory distress.
source: The only recorded side effect of purified CVF administration in rodents is transitory anaphylatoxin-mediated pulmonary inflammation resulting in acute respiratory distress (Proctor et al., 2006; Vogel and Fritzinger, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Proctor et al., 2006 and Vogel and Fritzinger, 2010.

claim: Respiratory distress was observed in some mice following the initial sub-conjunctival CVF injection.
source: In our hands, respiratory distress was observed in some mice following the initial sub-conjunctival CVF injection irrespective of group assignment (animals were euthanized).
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Topical CVF administration did not provoke respiratory or corneal abnormalities in any animals.
source: However, topical CVF administration did not provoke respiratory or corneal abnormalities in any animals.
evidence: This is an observation from the experiments.

claim: Topical CVF administration has no obvious effects on corneal health or transparency.
source: Previous findings also show that topical CVF administration has no obvious effects on corneal health or transparency (Zaidi et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zaidi et al., 2010.

claim: Experimental CVF administration was once thought to directly stimulate T cells, but such effects were later attributed to mitogen contamination.
source: Experimental CVF administration was once thought to directly stimulate T cells, but such effects were later attributed to mitogen contamination (Rumjanek et al., 1978; Cauvi et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rumjanek et al., 1978 and Cauvi et al., 2012.

claim: Highly-purified CVF from a commercial source was utilized for the studies.
source: Because our disease models were T cell-dependent, we utilized highly-purified CVF from a commercial source for our studies.
evidence: This describes a methodological choice to avoid contamination issues.

claim: There is no evidence to suggest that CVF impacted T cell responses outside of the eye.
source: Moreover, we found no evidence to suggest that CVF impacted T cell responses outside of the eye.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing no effects on T cell expansion in lymph nodes or blood.

claim: Local CVF treatment reduced corneal T cell infiltration following HSV-1 infection likely due to reduced inflammation overall in C3-depleted corneas.
source: Local CVF treatment reduced corneal T cell infiltration following HSV-1 infection (Figure 5G). However, this is likely due to reduced inflammation overall in C3-depleted corneas (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between reduced inflammation and reduced T cell infiltration.

claim: Ocular CVF treatment in the GVHD model did not impact the total numbers of T cells in the corneas at the experiment endpoint.
source: Likewise, ocular CVF treatment in the GVHD model did not impact on the total numbers of T cells in the corneas at the experiment endpoint.
evidence: This is supported by the data shown in Figure 8H.

claim: CVF treatment may delay the tempo of T cell influx into the cornea.
source: However, we have not excluded the possibility that CVF treatment may delay the tempo of T cell influx.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation of the study.

claim: CVF administration preserved corneal sensation in both HSV-1 and GVHD disease models.
source: Nonetheless, CVF administration preserved corneal sensation in both disease models.
evidence: This is supported by the experimental data from both models.

claim: Addressing C3 opens the door to future investigation to further elucidate the relevant pathomechanisms and corresponding therapeutic targets.
source: By addressing the 'heart' of the complement pathway (C3), this study opens the door to future investigation to further elucidate the relevant pathomechanisms and corresponding therapeutic targets.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of the study.

claim: The relevant complement activation pathways (classical, alternative, lectin, terminal), cellular targets, and impacts of anaphylatoxin receptor signaling are topics of future investigation.
source: The relevant complement activation pathways (classical, alternative, lectin, terminal), cellular targets, and impacts of anaphylatoxin receptor signaling are topics of future investigation.
evidence: This identifies future research directions.

claim: Complement activation is a double-edged sword in the cornea, as activation can be either protective or harmful.
source: Complement activation is a double-edged sword in the cornea, as activation can be either protective or harmful.
evidence: This is a synthesis of the findings showing both beneficial (viral clearance) and harmful (nerve damage) effects.

claim: Low-level complement turnover is observed in healthy corneas/tears.
source: Low-level complement turnover is observed in healthy corneas/tears, and complement may even contribute to the relative 'paucibacterial' state of the ocular surface microbiome (Doan et al., 2016; McDermott, 2013; Willcox et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Complement may contribute to the relative 'paucibacterial' state of the ocular surface microbiome.
source: Low-level complement turnover is observed in healthy corneas/tears, and complement may even contribute to the relative 'paucibacterial' state of the ocular surface microbiome (Doan et al., 2016; McDermott, 2013; Willcox et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The mechanisms regulating each complement-mediated effect in the cornea remain incompletely understood.
source: The mechanisms regulating each complement-mediated effect remain incompletely understood.
evidence: This identifies a knowledge gap.

claim: Elucidation of how complement activation is triggered, the relevant molecular mechanisms of its downstream signaling, and contributions to pathology will promote an important advancement in drug development for ocular surface disease.
source: Elucidation of how complement activation is triggered, the relevant molecular mechanisms of its downstream signaling, and contributions to pathology will promote an important advancement in drug development for ocular surface disease.
evidence: This is a statement about the implications of future research.

claim: Differences in complement regulation exist between mouse and man that will have to be resolved to assess the translational potential.
source: Animal models are necessary for mechanistic studies when it comes to understanding complement pathway regulation, especially in dynamic tissue microenvironments; however, differences in complement regulation exist between mouse and man that will also have to be resolved to further assess the translational potential (Jacobson and Weis, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Jacobson and Weis, 2008.

claim: Small nucleotide polymorphisms evoke changes in complement activity that have major impacts on disease risks.
source: Even among individual patients, small nucleotide polymorphisms evoke changes in complement activity that have major impacts on disease risks.
evidence: This reflects established knowledge about genetic variation in complement.

claim: Genetic linkages dubbed 'complotype' are important in differential susceptibility to AMD.
source: Such genetic linkages, dubbed 'complotype,' are important in differential susceptibility to AMD (Harris et al., 2012; Paun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harris et al., 2012 and Paun et al., 2016.

claim: Complotype differences may help explain differential susceptibility patterns in a variety of ocular surface diseases.
source: Accordingly, complotype differences may help explain differential susceptibility patterns in a variety of ocular surface diseases.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the AMD findings.

claim: The data have demonstrated successful prophylactic intervention in repressing complement-mediated sensory nerve pathology in two experimental T cell-dependent corneal disease models.
source: Our data herein have demonstrated successful prophylactic intervention in repressing complement-mediated sensory nerve pathology in two well characterized experimental T cell-dependent corneal disease models.
evidence: This is a summary of the CVF treatment results.

claim: Future investigation is needed to determine the efficacy of therapeutic intervention on established ocular surface diseases.
source: Other avenues of future investigation are also needed to determine the efficacy of therapeutic intervention on established ocular surface diseases.
evidence: This identifies a limitation and future direction.

claim: Successful implementation of complement-targeted therapeutics for topical ophthalmic use may provide the benefit of controlling insidious ocular surface diseases without the risks associated with systemic therapies.
source: Successful implementation of complement-targeted therapeutics for topical ophthalmic use may provide the benefit of controlling insidious ocular surface diseases without the risks associated with systemic therapies.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential clinical benefits.
